chapter_theme: The man praises her beauty through deliberate hyperbole, defeating the standard comparisons: flowers, the moon, swan's down. As the praise goes on, it becomes a claim of exclusivity, and what is seen by many ceases to compare with what he alone sees.
structure_note: The chapter's movement is by comparison: softness and flowers (1111-1115), the moon (1116-1119), softness again in the feet (1120). Parimelazhagar sets 1116-1119 at a night tryst with the moon overhead.

1111.reading: The man addresses the anicham flower, granting it delicacy and telling it that the woman he loves is more delicate still.
1111.nuance: வாழி sounds like a blessing, but for Parimelazhagar it is a polite way to end the flower's pride: stop thinking you are the softest. He also says the man has just touched her, so the praise comes from touch and not sight.

1112.reading: The man scolds his heart for reeling whenever it sees flowers, supposing that her eyes resemble what anyone can look at.

positions.position: The flowers don't match her eyes, and the heart is rebuked for its false comparison now that he alone has seen them.
positions.quote: அம்மலர்கள் ஒவ்வாமை கண்டு, ஒப்புமை கருதிய நெஞ்சை இகழ்ந்து கூறியவாறு.

positions.position: Her eyes match flowers in colour but not in quality.
The verse is direct praise: her eyes are indeed a flower that many see and admire.

1113.reading: The man describes her: bamboo shoulders, a body like young shoots, pearl teeth, fragrance, and kohl-lined eyes that are spears.
1113.nuance: Parimelazhagar offers a witty setting as an alternative: her friend claims not to know whom he means, so this list is a description for identifying her. Everything in it is soft except the eyes, the one weapon among the delights, as in chapter 109.

1114.reading: The man says that if blue water-lilies could see, they would bow their heads and look at the ground, saying they can't match the eyes of this finely jewelled woman.
1114.nuance: The lilies would take the posture of a modest woman, which is the very gesture she makes in 1094. Parimelazhagar draws out the unstated corollary: lacking sight and shame, real lilies stand proudly staring at the sky.

1115.reading: The man says that she has worn anicham flowers without removing their stems, so no good drums will sound for her waist.
1115.nuance: This is a mock funeral. As Parimelazhagar spells it out, the stems' weight will snap her waist, and then only the drum for the dead will sound. Praise by imagined catastrophe is one of the book's boldest jokes. He glosses கால் as the flower's bud or stalk end, and Manakkudavar as its stems.

1116.reading: The man says the stars have strayed from their places, unable to tell the moon from the young woman's face.
1116.nuance: This gives a fanciful explanation for why stars move at all: they are lost. Manakkudavar says so directly, that the poet presents their motion as confusion.

1117.reading: The man asks whether a woman's face has spots, as the bright moon does when it fills out its lost parts.
1117.nuance: This undoes the previous verse. Waning and spots should have told the stars the difference, so Parimelazhagar hears mockery of the stars: they had every means of knowing, and still failed.

1118.reading: The man tells the moon that if it could shine as her face does, it too could be loved.
1118.nuance: வாழி varies in force: Parimelazhagar calls it agreement when spoken to the flower in 1111 and contempt here, because the moon's spots make the condition impossible. Manakkudavar treats it as an empty particle. The tone of the verse depends on that small word.

1119.reading: The man tells the moon that if it wants to resemble the face of the flower-eyed woman, it must not appear where many can see it.
1119.nuance: The criterion has moved from brightness to privacy. For Parimelazhagar, what disqualifies the moon is that it shows itself to everyone, while he alone has fully enjoyed her face. Praise here shades into possession.

1120.reading: The man says anicham flowers and swan's down are to her feet what the nerunji fruit is.
1120.nuance: The verse says நெருஞ்சிப் பழம், the fruit, and Kalaignar and Pope turn it into a thorn. Parimelazhagar explains the choice of fruit, since it is hard at the tip.

positions.position: This is a covert refusal: her friend has proposed elopement, and feet like these couldn't cross the wilderness.
positions.quote: உடன் போக்கு உரைத்த தோழிக்கு அதனது அருமை கூறி மறுத்தது.

positions.position: It is plain praise: her feet are softer than these.

links.note: 957 uses the moon's spot to say the flaws of the high-born show as conspicuously as a mark on the moon. 1117 uses the same spot in praise of an unblemished face. In one, a mark reveals a failing; in the other, its absence is the point.
The lily in 1114 would bow and look at the ground, as the woman herself does in 1094. The lily is imagined acting out the shame of being outdone, in a gesture she makes for love.
Both disqualify a comparison because it is பலர் காணும், seen by many. What starts as a heart scolded about flowers becomes an instruction to the moon, showing how his praise rests on exclusivity.

source_issues: 1113: Parimelazhagar offers two settings for the verse, the man speaking to his own friend or to her friend, so its addressee is open even within one commentary.
